newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: General Assembly adopts Libyan draft aimed at U.S..
newsitem.headline: General Assembly adopts Libyan draft aimed at U.S..

text.p: The General Assembly on Wednesday adopted a Libyan resolution, directed against the United States, calling for the immediate repeal of laws that unilaterally impose penalties on companies and citizens of other countries.
The vote was 56 to four, with the unusually large number of 76 abstentions.
Among countries voting for the Libyan resolution were China and Russia. The United States was joined by Israel, Micronesia and Uzbekistan in voting against the measure.
President Bill Clinton signed legislation earlier this year punishing foreign firms that invest in energy projects in Libya and Iran on the grounds that they support terrorism.

The assembly vote contrasted with one on a similar Cuban resolution earlier this month, calling for an end to the three-decade-old U.S. embargo against Havana, that was approved by 137 to three with 25 abstentions.
Like the Cuban resolution, the Libyan draft sought to target U.S. laws that make other countries' companies and individuals liable to penalties if they violate unilaterally-imposed U.S. sanctions.

A major difference is that, while Cuba is not subject to U.N. sanctions, Libya has been the target since 1992 of sanctions imposed by the Security Council over the 1988 bombing of Pan Am flight 103 over Lockerbie, Scotland, which killed 270 people, and of a French UTA airliner over Niger in 1989 which claimed 171 lives.

Deputy U.S. representative Edward Gnehm said Libya was trying to make U.N. members believe that "this resolution is about free trade and the right of states to choose their own models of economic development."

"It is not," he said. "It is aimed at distracting attention from Libya's obstinate refusal to comply with its obligations...imposed because of Libya's involvement in two terrorist bombings of civilian aircraft."

On behalf of the European Union, whose 15 members supported the Cuban resolution but abstained on the Libyan draft, Irish diplomat Michael Hoey repeated EU opposition to legislation which purported to apply to other countries, in violation of their sovereignty.

"The European Union must, however, make a firm and unmistakable distinction between measures imposed unilaterally by individual states, and those which are undertaken with the full authority of the Security Council and in conformity with the Charter of the United Nations," he said.
